analysis.title: 10 for the Weekend (Dioni Ellinikaki, GS Gen Sales), 6 Nov 2026
key_insights: GS describes the week as COVID/GFC type price action as markets repriced the post blue sweep growth and policy outlook, with the AI trade at the center of the move.

US ETF shorts rose 7%, the third largest increase in five years. Single stock degrossing was modest at 0.5 SD, so per GS Prime data discretionary HFs were not the main driver of Thursday's price action.
Anecdotal feedback from fundamental clients suggests thematic AI tilts had already been reduced during last week's risk off.
Global Fundamental L/S fell 1.3% Thursday. TMT L/S fell more than 4% and is roughly flat YTD versus +24% before the summer AI selloff. Systematic L/S gained 0.2% and is +16% YTD.

HF gross leverage is 314%, the 97th percentile versus five years, so there may be room for more risk reduction. Part of this reflects mark to market, since fund equity has fallen faster than gross market value.

The market traded four AI concerns: insufficient capital to finance the buildout, insufficient revenues to justify investment, insufficient power and permitting capacity, and an unsustainable aggregate spending trajectory. GS notes constrained supply does not mean disappearing demand.

SOX multiples are compressed roughly 50% from the June/July highs. The next debate is how much execution risk is priced in. Narrative changes would come from political reflexivity around AI investment, stabilization in funding markets, and evidence that spending, compute demand and revenues remain intact (Rich Privo).

GS Economics does not see the Senate result substantially changing the policy outlook, though larger Democratic majorities increase leverage around fiscal deadlines. Reversing last year's spending cuts could add roughly 0.25% of GDP to 2027 spending, with 11 December the first key funding deadline.

GIR expects tighter state and local scrutiny of data centres (grid costs, power availability, consumer protections) but expects the issue to fade and any moratoria to be short lived. It sees a state by state issue rather than a federal stop, and 2027 capacity looks largely locked in.

GS estimates hyperscaler capex of $1.2tn in 2027 and $1.4tn in 2028, $130bn and $100bn above consensus. Growth slows from nearly 100% in 2026 to 54% in 2027 and 12% in 2028. GS says it is too early for the sell side to materially cut estimates.

Eric Sheridan's work estimates the six major US hyperscalers need roughly $1.42tn of cumulative AI revenues across 2028 to 2030, about $11.6bn of annual revenue per GW, to earn a 15% ROIC on 2026 to 2027 investment.

GS Economics estimates AI investment at around $1tn globally in 2026, rising from 0.9% of global GDP in 2026 to 1.4% by 2028. A haircut to the 2028 buildout would become a growth question, especially with higher energy costs and tighter financial conditions.
GS Spec Sales best ideas in Europe: long Rolls Royce, sell Kuehne & Nagel, long Orange, short Munich Re.

tension_points.bull_case: GS estimates 2027 and 2028 hyperscaler capex above consensus ($1.2tn and $1.4tn), 2027 capacity is largely locked in, and constrained supply does not mean disappearing demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Four concerns: funding, revenues, power and permitting, and an unsustainable spending trajectory. Capex growth slows from nearly 100% to 54% to 12%, and the revenue needed for a 15% ROIC is $1.42tn cumulative across 2028 to 2030.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that underlying spending, compute demand and revenues are not intact, or stabilization in funding markets failing to occur.
